name: Meal prep and personal chef
what_example: weekly meal prep in North Hills

crowd.buyer: Busy families and couples who want home-cooked dinners
not_yet: Don't sell meals cooked in your own kitchen until you've checked your state's cottage food and health rules.
Don't give diet or health advice: cook to what the client tells you.
Don't rent a commercial kitchen before you have 4 regular clients.
crowd.note: Trust first: a free kitchen visit before any cook day. Groceries go on the bill at cost.
crowd.basis: Scores, buyer, first $1 and not-yet lines: research/niches/mealprep.json crowd_scores (our judgment, with the BLS projection for private household cooks behind growing). Best months: all year, our judgment, since dinners are needed every week.

safety: Cook in the client's own kitchen with groceries bought for them. Selling meals cooked in your home kitchen falls under state cottage food and health rules, and Florida's, for one, covers only foods that don't need time or temperature control. Check your city and state.

Get every food allergy in writing on the paper intake before the first cook day, and keep it there: the week menu needs only the foods to leave out. Read every package label for those foods when you shop.
Fridge at 40°F or below and freezer at 0°F or below, and everything you cook goes in within 2 hours.
Cook to the FDA safe temperatures with a food thermometer, and label every container with its eat-by date, reheat steps (to 165°F) and allergens.
Take a food handler course before your first cook day (ServSafe's online course is $15 and the certificate lasts three years). Rules for personal chefs vary, so check your city and state.
Get liability insurance before your first paid cook day.
Never give diet or health advice. Cook to what the client tells you, and if a doctor or dietitian gave them a meal plan, cook from that plan.

extra.title: Kitchen visit script (20 minutes, free)
lines: 1. Thanks for having me. Could you show me the kitchen: oven, stove, pots and pans, and where things go?
2. Who eats at home, and does anyone have a food allergy? How serious is it? I write every allergy down and read every label for it when I shop.
3. How do you like to eat? Anything you avoid, and any favorites? I cook to what you tell me, and I don't give diet advice.
4. Let me check the fridge and freezer with my thermometer: 40°F or below and 0°F or below.
5. How many dinners a week, for how many people, and which day works for me to cook here?
6. Groceries: I shop the morning of and bill them at cost with the receipt, or you shop from my list.
7. My founding price is {founding}. Want to set the first cook day?

offer.name: Weekly cook day in your kitchen
offer.range_text: $200 to $500 per cook day, groceries extra
offer.basis: From research/niches/mealprep.json, checked 2026-10-19: APPCA's personal chefs report $200 to $500 a day, usually one client a day, and Sous puts 4 meals a week for a family of 4 at about $263 plus groceries. Groceries run $60 to $200 a week on top (Care.com). Where you sit in the range is our judgment.

sources.publisher: American Personal and Private Chef Association (APPCA)
sources.says: Its personal chefs report $200 to $500 a day depending on the market. They plan, purchase and prepare meals, usually once a week, in the client's home or a rented professional kitchen, and serve several clients, usually one per day.
For a family of 4 who wants 4 meals per week, the average cost is $262.79 plus groceries.
The average posted rate for a personal chef is $24.20 to $31.05 per hour, not including groceries, which typically cost an additional $60 to $200 per week.

steps: Free kitchen visit: I see your kitchen, and we go over allergies, the way you eat and what you love.

On cook day I shop, then cook, pack and label in your kitchen, and clean up.
Dinners go in your fridge and freezer with the eat-by date and reheat steps on every label.

offer.promise_note: I can't promise how anyone's diet or health will change, and I don't give diet advice. I promise the cooking: every dinner as planned, recipes planned around the allergies you list, a label on every container and a clean kitchen.

ai_rules: Every new client starts with a free kitchen visit. That is the next step.
Never promise health, weight or diet results, and never give diet or medical advice: cook to what the client says, and if a doctor or dietitian gave them a meal plan, cook from that plan.
Never say a dish is safe for an allergy. Say the recipe leaves it out and every package label gets read.
Groceries are billed separately at cost. Say any price once, exactly as given.

sources.says: A cottage food product means food that is not time or temperature controlled for safety or a potentially hazardous food.
A food manager certification is not required for most personal chef businesses operating at a client's home, but members must have proof of completing a food handler certificate course.

objections.label: Can you cook around an allergy?
objections.means: Someone at home has a food allergy, and they want to know you'll take it seriously.
objections.answer: Thanks for telling me. Every allergy goes on the intake form in writing, the recipes leave it out, I read every package label for it when I shop, and every container says what the dish contains. If it's severe, tell me at the kitchen visit and we'll plan around it together.
objections.next: Book the kitchen visit and get the allergy in writing first.
objections.check: Only take on an allergy you can keep out of the recipes, and never promise a dish is free of it.

sources.says: The major food allergens are milk, eggs, fish, Crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans and sesame (the 9th since January 1, 2023). Labels must name the food source of each, and people with food allergies should read labels.

objections.label: Are groceries included?
objections.means: They want to know what the groceries add.
objections.answer: Good question. Groceries are billed separately at cost, with the receipt, so you pay what the food costs and nothing more. I shop the morning of each cook day, or you can shop from my list.
objections.next: Say how groceries work, then offer the kitchen visit.

sources.says: Personal chef rates don't include groceries, which typically cost an additional $60 to $200 per week.

sources.publisher: American Personal and Private Chef Association (APPCA)
sources.says: Personal chefs plan, purchase and prepare meals, usually once a week, either at the client's home or in a rented professional kitchen.

objections.label: Why not a meal kit or takeout?
objections.means: They're comparing you with meal kits or takeout.
objections.answer: Fair question, and those work for lots of people. With me nothing needs cooking on a weeknight: the dinners are made in your kitchen, around your allergies and what you like, and ready to reheat.

objections.label: Can you cook at your place and drop off?
objections.means: They'd like meals made somewhere else and brought over.
objections.answer: I cook in your kitchen with groceries bought for you. Selling meals cooked in my own home kitchen falls under state cottage food and health rules, and in states like Florida those cover only foods that don't need the fridge. So I cook at your place, and you can see how everything is made.
objections.check: Check your city and state rules before you ever sell food made in your own kitchen.

sources.says: A cottage food product means food that is not time or temperature controlled for safety or a potentially hazardous food.

sources.publisher: Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services
sources.says: Unlicensed home kitchens may make certain low-risk foods for sale: breads, cakes and cookies, candies, honey, jams, fruit pies, dry herbs, homemade pasta, granola, nuts, vinegars and popcorn.

objections.label: Can you cook for my diet?
objections.means: They follow a diet, or want food that fits a health goal.
objections.answer: Happy to cook the way you like to eat, from what you tell me. I don't give diet or health advice, so if a doctor or dietitian gave you a meal plan, share it and I'll cook from that plan.
objections.next: Ask what they eat and avoid, then offer the kitchen visit.

objections.label: Are you certified and insured?
objections.means: They want to know you're trained and covered.
objections.answer: Good question to ask. I hold a food handler certificate and carry liability insurance, and I'm glad to send you both before the kitchen visit.
objections.next: Send the certificate and the insurance page, then book the kitchen visit.
objections.check: Only send this once you have the certificate and your policy is active.

sources.says: A food manager certification is not required for most personal chef businesses operating at a client's home, but members must have proof of completing a food handler certificate course.
The ServSafe Food Handler online course and assessment costs $15.00, and the certificate is valid for three years.

objections.label: How long does it keep?
objections.means: They want to know how long the food keeps.
objections.answer: Every container has a label with its eat-by date and reheat steps. Cooked dinners keep 3 to 4 days in the fridge, so the later dinners go in the freezer and move to the fridge the night before.

sources.says: Refrigerator at 40°F: soups and stews, cooked meat and poultry dishes and cooked fish keep 3 to 4 days. Food kept frozen at 0°F stays safe; freezer times are for quality.

sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.says: Refrigerate leftovers promptly, and eat them within 3 to 4 days.

objections.label: Too much for us
objections.means: The price is a stretch for them.
objections.answer: That's fair. Two ways to make it work: a half cook day with 2 dinners, or 4 cook days booked ahead for a little less each time. Groceries stay at cost either way.
objections.next: Hold your price. Offer the half cook day or 4 booked ahead.

win.title: Log the new client
win.description: A client said yes: logs the win in your Pipeline, writes the booking message, the prep message and the day-before reminder, and a printable first cook day checklist.
win.booking: Hi {greet}, you're all set! Your first cook day is {when}. It's {deal}. I'll send the menu for your okay a few days before, and every container gets a label with the eat-by date and reheat steps.{pay}
win.prep: Before the first cook day, could you fill in the kitchen intake form I'm sending (allergies, the way you eat, foods you avoid and your kitchen), and clear a fridge shelf and some freezer space? I'll bring containers and a food thermometer.
win.reminder: Hi {greet}, see you {when} for your cook day. I'll shop that morning. Reply here if anything changes, especially an allergy.
win.founding: Founding client: after two cook days, ask {greet} for honest feedback you may quote as a founding client, and ask before you post any photo of their food or kitchen. Never ask for a review in exchange.

Kitchen visit: Get the intake form filled in: every food allergy and how serious it is, the way they eat, foods they avoid and favorites.
Check the fridge (40°F or below) and the freezer (0°F or below) with an appliance thermometer.
Look over the oven, stove, pans, containers and the room in the fridge and freezer.
Agree on groceries: you shop and bill at cost with the receipt, or they shop from your list.
Agree on how you get in, and on your cancellation terms.
Cook day: Wash your hands for at least 20 seconds before you start and after touching raw meat, poultry, seafood or eggs.
Read every package label for the foods to leave out before it goes in the cart.
Keep raw meat, poultry and seafood away from ready-to-eat food, with their own cutting board.
Cook each dish to its safe temperature, checked with a food thermometer.
Divide into shallow containers and into the fridge or freezer within 2 hours.
Label every container: dish, eat-by date, reheat steps and allergens.
Clean up and leave the menu card on the fridge.
After: Send the menu text with the reheat steps.
Ask what to change for next week.
Invoice the cook day and the groceries, with the receipt.

sources.says: Clean, separate, cook and chill: wash hands, keep raw meat away from ready-to-eat food, cook to safe temperatures checked with a food thermometer, and refrigerate within 2 hours.

sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.says: Wash hands for at least 20 seconds, keep the refrigerator at 40°F or below and the freezer at 0°F or below, and refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.
Labels must name the food source of each of the 9 major allergens, and people with food allergies should read labels.
